name: Kunjen

catalog_citation: Sommer, B.A. (1969). Kunjen Phonology: Synchronic and Diachronic. Pacific Linguistics Series B, No. 11. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-B11 (PDF via sealang.net PL archive).
catalog_locator: pp. 29-30, section 2.1 Oykangand, 'Stress Pattern' (also p. 28 section 2.0 and p. 31 section 2.2 for dialects)
catalog_quote: For most Australian languages, stress occurs regularly according to a predictable pattern (Capell 1956, 1967:104; Hale E:2; Oates 1964:18-19), usually on the initial syllable of the word. By contrast, there is evidence in Kunjen for a strong phonological pressure against this stress pattern. Stress is not predictable in the case of words of more than two syllables. Stress on monosyllabic words is discernible when these occur within phonological phrases of more than one word. ... Words of two syllables are invariably stressed on the final syllable: intYim 'house', amay 'big' ... Words of three syllables may be stressed on either the ultimate or penultimate syllable. A survey of dictionary entries revealed no statistically preferred pattern: the two word types were numerically almost identical. Although no two lexical items in the language are differentiated solely on the basis of stress,…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the dialect-exceptions quote are all present verbatim in the PL-B11 text we hold at the stated pages (28, 29-30, 31-32); only scanned letter-spacing differs. (2) The deciding source is a dedicated 76-pp phonology monograph by the principal fieldworker with an explicit stress subsection grounded in a dictionary count; nothing in Glottolog's list or in what could be checked online (ANU Open Research, Crossref, Glottolog; (3) The classification 'lexical stress within a right-edge three-syllable window, disyllables final, not Australian initial stress' follows directly from the quoted text; StressTyp2's U;P is a coarser rendering of the same source. (4) One refinement surfaced: Blevins 200

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: No stress statement anywhere in the volume (a full-text search for stress/accent returns only non-linguistic uses). Appendix 1 gives the segment inventory 'formally attested in Sommer (1969)' and says 'The shape of Oykangand syllables and words has been a matter of debate; the reader is referred to Sommer (1969) for the initial analysis, and to the reply from Sommer (1981)'. Confirms Sommer 1969 remains the author's own phonology of record.

sources.note: Per Blevins 2001:485, pp. 86-87 discuss stress placement across the Kunjen dialects (Rigsby's Olgol with consistent V2 stress; Uw-El with root-initial stress) — the only other first-hand-informed statement on Kunjen stress, and it bears on whether the 'lexical, right-edge window' coding from Oykangand holds for the whole kunj1245 languoid.
